questions.question: A three-voter etcd cluster loses one voting member. How many live voters remain, and can writes still commit?
options: Two remain; writes can commit because two is the majority
Two remain; writes stop because all three voters are required
One remains; writes can commit through the leader alone
One remains; serializable reads require a new election
questions.explanation: A three-voter cluster has a quorum of two. One voter can be unavailable while the remaining two still elect a leader and commit writes.

questions.question: What is the main trade-off of an explicitly serializable etcd read?
options: It encrypts the value but cannot return a revision
It is served only by the leader and therefore costs more
It can use local member state with lower coordination cost but may be stale
It bypasses MVCC and can observe partial transactions
questions.explanation: Serializable reads can be served from a member's local applied state without a live quorum round trip. They preserve etcd's serializable ordering but may trail the latest quorum-committed revision.

questions.question: A watcher reconnects from a revision that etcd has already compacted. What is the correct client recovery?
options: Replace one cluster member to recover the old watch events
Rebuild state with a current range read, record its revision, and resume watching
Defragment every member until the old events return
Switch the watch to a serializable read mode
questions.explanation: Compacted event history cannot be replayed. The client must discard its incomplete cache, obtain a complete current snapshot and revision, then establish a new watch boundary.

questions.question: Why is a lease-backed ownership key insufficient by itself to protect an external database mutation?
options: Leases cannot be attached to keys
Lease expiry does not stop a paused or partitioned old process from acting externally
Leases require all cluster members to be leaders
Lease keys are excluded from transactions
questions.explanation: An old process can continue after its lease is lost. The protected resource needs a fencing token, idempotency rule, or transaction that rejects stale owners.

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes compaction from defragmentation?
options: Compaction removes current keys; defragmentation recreates deleted watch events
Compaction discards old MVCC history; defragmentation returns reusable backend pages to the filesystem
Compaction changes cluster membership; defragmentation changes the Raft leader
Both operations are replicated and non-blocking on every member
questions.explanation: Compaction makes older revisions unavailable and reusable inside the backend. Defragmentation rebuilds one member's backend so reusable pages reduce the physical file size, and live defrag blocks that member while it runs.

questions.question: Write latency rises together with etcd_disk_wal_fsync_duration_seconds. Which response addresses the primary bottleneck?
options: Repair or replace the slow durable storage path while preserving quorum
Increase watch history retention
Switch every client to one endpoint
Add large values so each transaction does more work
questions.explanation: Raft commits are bounded by peer network latency and durable disk persistence. A slow WAL fsync path must be repaired or replaced; unrelated keyspace changes do not remove that physical latency.

questions.question: Why add a new member as a learner before promoting it to a voter?
options: A learner can serve as two votes during catch-up
A learner can catch up without increasing quorum before it is ready
A learner disables TLS while copying data
A learner permanently replaces the need for odd voter counts
questions.explanation: A learner replicates state but does not vote. It can catch up without immediately changing the majority requirement, then be promoted after health and replication evidence pass.

questions.question: A voting majority is permanently lost and cannot be recovered. What establishes a safe replacement cluster?
options: A runtime member-add request sent to the unavailable minority
A serializable read from any surviving old member
A tested snapshot restored into fenced replacement members with new cluster identity
Defragmenting the surviving data directory until a leader appears
questions.explanation: Without quorum, runtime membership cannot authorize a new majority. Disaster recovery restores an approved snapshot into a new cluster and member identity, then verifies RPO, revisions, security, and dependent-client reconciliation.
